blocks.text: Questions on what this page has just taught. Choose one answer for each.

questions.stem: Per this page, thread T1 sets a plain field `x = 1`, and a second later by the clock thread T2 reads `x`. What decides whether T2 is guaranteed to read `1`?

options.text: That the write ran earlier than the read by the clock
options.says: The page says happens-before does not mean the write physically occurred before the read on the clock.

options.text: That a happens-before edge orders the write before the read
options.says: The page says a read is guaranteed to see a write only when the write happens-before it; unordered actions have a non-deterministic outcome.

options.text: That the read runs in a loop that keeps reading the field
options.says: The page's broken flag reads a plain field in a loop and warns it might loop forever due to caching, so re-reading guarantees nothing.

origin.section: The Difference Between Happens-before and Wall-clock Time

questions.stem: Per this page, why does the Initialization-on-Demand Holder's `getInstance()` need no lock?

options.text: Because `INSTANCE` is volatile, so each read sees the latest write
options.says: The page's holder declares INSTANCE static final, not volatile; its safety comes from the static initializer rule.

options.text: Because `getInstance()` is static, so calls to it run one at a time
options.says: The page does not say static methods run one at a time; getInstance() has no synchronization at all.

options.text: Because the class initializer happens-before any use of the class
options.says: The page says a class's static initializer happens-before the first access to its static fields, which underpins the holder idiom.

concepts: Happens-before is about visibility, not about which action ran first on the clock.
A class's static initializer happens-before any use of the class, which makes the holder idiom a safe lazy singleton.
